PROG1.title: C++ Programming Fundamentals
PROG1.summary: C++ is a general-purpose programming language widely used for software development, systems programming, games, embedded systems, and other performance-intensive applications.

sections.heading: What is C++?
paragraphs: C++ is a general-purpose programming language widely used for software development, systems programming, games, embedded systems, and other performance-intensive applications.

It supports multiple programming paradigms, specifically procedural programming (organising instructions into procedures and functions) and object-oriented programming (organising programs around classes and objects).
Learning C++ provides a strong foundation in programming fundamentals (such as variables, loops, and functions) that easily transfer to other languages.

sections.heading: Basic C++ Program Structure
paragraphs: An example of a basic program structure is:
list: Key Components – The structure relies on a header file (#include <iostream>), a namespace (using namespace std;), the main() function, statements, and a return statement.
The main() Function – This function serves as the absolute starting point of execution for every C++ program.
C++ Statements – These are instructions that tell the program to perform an action. Most C++ statements must end with a semicolon (;).
Output with cout – Part of the iostream header, cout displays output on the screen using the insertion operator (<<). It can display single or multiple combined values.
Single-line comments – Notes written in the source code to help programmers understand the logic. They are completely ignored by the compiler and begin with //.
Multi-line comments – Notes written in the source code to help programmers understand the logic. They are completely ignored by the compiler and are enclosed within /* and */.

sections.heading: Variables, Data Types, and Constants
paragraphs: Constants: Declared using the const keyword, constants hold values that cannot be changed after they are defined, which prevents accidental modifications to fixed values.
list: Variables – Named storage locations used to store and manipulate data in a program.
Variable Naming Rules – Use meaningful names that describe the data (e.g., studentAge), do not use spaces, do not begin names with a number, and do not use C++ reserved keywords.
int – Whole numbers (e.g., 20).
float / double – Decimal numbers, with double offering greater precision.
char – A single character enclosed in single quotes (e.g., 'A').
string – Text enclosed in double quotes (e.g., "Maria").
bool – Boolean values representing true or false.

sections.heading: C++ Operators
list: Arithmetic Operators – Used to perform mathematical calculations: + (Addition), - (Subtraction), * (Multiplication), / (Division), and % (Modulus/Remainder).
Assignment Operators – Used to assign or update variable values: = (Assignment), += (Add and assign), -= (Subtract and assign), *= (Multiply and assign), and /= (Divide and assign).

Comparison Operators – Compare values and return a true or false result: == (Equal to), != (Not equal to), > (Greater than), < (Less than), >= (Greater than or equal to), and <= (Less than or equal to).
Logical Operators – Combine or reverse conditional states: && (AND — both conditions must be true), || (OR — at least one condition must be true), and ! (NOT — reverses the condition).

sections.heading: The Input-Process-Output (IPO) Model
list: Input – Receives data from the user utilizing cin and the extraction operator (>>).
Process – Performs calculations or applies programming logic to the inputs.
Output – Displays the processed results to the screen using cout.

sections.heading: Control Structures & Basic Logic
list: if statement – Executes a specific block of code only when the given condition evaluates to true.
if-else statement – Provides two distinct execution paths (one if the condition is true, and another if it is false).
else if ladder – Allows the program to test multiple consecutive conditions.
Arrays – Used to store multiple values of the exact same data type in a single variable. Array elements are accessed using zero-based indexing (where the first element is at index 0).
for loop – Repeats a block of code a specific, pre-determined number of times.
while loop – Repeats a block of code as long as a specified condition remains true. An update statement inside the loop is necessary to prevent infinite loops.
Functions – Reusable blocks of code written to perform a singular, specific task. They can declare parameters to receive external values, which are supplied as arguments when the function is called.

sections.heading: Common Beginner Errors & Debugging
paragraphs: Debugging is the procedural process of identifying and correcting errors in your code.
list: Typical Beginner Mistakes – Missing semicolons (;).
Typical Beginner Mistakes – Misspelled keywords or using undeclared variables.
Typical Beginner Mistakes – Incorrect variable declarations or mismatched quotation marks.
Typical Beginner Mistakes – Using incorrect comparison operators (such as confusing = with ==).
Typical Beginner Mistakes – Missing braces { } or setting incorrect loop conditions.

PROG2.title: Basic Syntax and Control Structures
PROG2.summary: Syntax refers to the rules for writing valid C++ code.

sections.heading: What is C++ Syntax?
paragraphs: Syntax refers to the rules for writing valid C++ code.
The compiler checks whether the program follows the language syntax.
list: Keywords – Common syntax element.
Identifiers – Common syntax element.
Operators – Common syntax element.
Braces { } – Common syntax element.
Parentheses ( ) – Common syntax element.
Semicolons ; – Common syntax element.
Statements and expressions – Common syntax element.

sections.heading: Basic C++ Program Format
paragraphs: The braces define the body of main().

sections.heading: Semicolons
paragraphs: Most C++ statements end with a semicolon (;).
Missing a semicolon can cause a compilation error.

sections.heading: Braces { }
paragraphs: Braces group statements into a block.
The statements inside { } belong to the if structure.

sections.heading: Parentheses ( )
paragraphs: Parentheses are used in conditions, function calls, and expressions.

sections.heading: Comments and Readability
paragraphs: Comments explain code and make programs easier to understand.
Readable code uses meaningful names and consistent formatting.

sections.heading: C++ Statements and Expressions
paragraphs: A statement is an instruction executed by the program.

sections.heading: Sequential Control Structure
paragraphs: Sequence is the simplest control structure.
Statements execute from top to bottom in the order written.

sections.heading: Activity: Trace a Sequence
paragraphs: What is the value of z after addition?
What is the final value of z?

sections.heading: Control Structures
paragraphs: Control structures determine the order in which statements execute.
These structures form the foundation of program logic.
list: Sequence – execute statements in order.
Selection – choose between alternatives.
Repetition – repeat statements.

sections.heading: Selection: If Statement
paragraphs: The if statement executes a block when a condition is true.
If the condition is false, the block is skipped.

sections.heading: If–Else
paragraphs: Exactly one of the two blocks executes.

sections.heading: Else If
paragraphs: else if allows several conditions to be checked.

sections.heading: Nested If
paragraphs: A nested if is an if statement placed inside another if statement.
Nested decisions should be used carefully to keep logic readable.

sections.heading: Activity: Decision Making
paragraphs: Write a C++ program that asks for a student's grade.
Challenge: Add a condition that checks whether the entered grade is between 0 and 100.
list: 90 or above – Excellent
75–89 – Passed
Below 75 – Failed

sections.heading: Switch Statement
paragraphs: switch is useful when one expression is compared with several fixed values.

sections.heading: Break and Default in Switch
paragraphs: break stops execution of the current switch case.
default executes when no case matches.
break helps prevent unintended execution of following cases.

sections.heading: Switch Activity
paragraphs: Ask the user for a choice and use switch to display the selected operation.
Challenge: connect the menu to two input numbers.
list: 1 – Add
2 – Subtract
3 – Multiply
4 – Divide

sections.heading: Repetition / Loops
paragraphs: Repetition allows a program to execute a block multiple times.
The appropriate loop depends on when and how the repetition condition is evaluated.
list: for – Common C++ loop
while – Common C++ loop
do-while – Common C++ loop

sections.heading: For Loop
paragraphs: A for loop is commonly used when the number of repetitions is known or controlled by a counter.

sections.heading: For Loop Flow
list: Initialize i – Step in for loop flow
Test condition – Step in for loop flow
Execute body – Step in for loop flow
Update i – Step in for loop flow
Repeat while condition is true – Step in for loop flow

sections.heading: Activity: For Loop
paragraphs: Then modify it to display only even numbers.
Display the multiplication table of a number entered by the user.

sections.heading: While Loop
paragraphs: A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true.
The condition is tested before each iteration.

sections.heading: While Loop: Important Rule
paragraphs: Make sure the loop condition can eventually become false.
The update i++ prevents an unintended infinite loop.

sections.heading: Do-While Loop
paragraphs: A do-while loop executes the body at least once.
Condition is checked after the loop body.

sections.heading: While vs Do-While
list: Condition is checked first – while feature
Body may execute zero times – while feature
Body executes first – do-while feature
Condition is checked afterward – do-while feature
Body executes at least once – do-while feature

sections.heading: Continue Statement
paragraphs: continue skips the current iteration and moves to the next iteration.

sections.heading: Break vs Continue
paragraphs: Use them when they make program logic clearer.
list: Stops the entire loop – break description
Skips the current iteration – continue description
Continues with the next iteration – continue description

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
list: Syntax provides the rules for writing valid C++ programs. – Key Takeaway
Statements normally end with semicolons. – Key Takeaway
Braces group statements into blocks. – Key Takeaway
Sequence executes statements in order. – Key Takeaway
Selection uses if, else if, else, and switch. – Key Takeaway
Repetition uses for, while, and do-while. – Key Takeaway
break terminates a loop or switch. – Key Takeaway
continue skips the current loop iteration. – Key Takeaway
Control structures allow programs to solve more complex problems. – Key Takeaway

PROG3.title: Functions
PROG3.summary: A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a specific task.

sections.heading: WHAT IS A FUNCTION?
paragraphs: A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a specific task.
Functions allow a program to divide a large problem into smaller, manageable tasks.
Instead of writing the same instructions repeatedly, a function can be called whenever the task is needed.

sections.heading: WHY USE FUNCTIONS?
paragraphs: Functions also reduce code repetition and support modular programming.
list: Organized
Reusable
Easier to understand
Easier to test
Easier to debug

sections.heading: BASIC FUNCTION SYNTAX
paragraphs: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

sections.heading: PARTS OF A FUNCTION
list: Return type – the type of value returned.
Function name – identifies the function.
Parameters – values received by the function.
Function body – statements executed by the function.
Return statement – sends a value back to the caller when needed.

sections.heading: FUNCTION DEFINITION
paragraphs: A function definition contains the actual code that performs the task.
Example: void displayMessage() { cout << "Welcome to C++!"; }
The function above does not return a value, so its return type is void.

sections.heading: CALLING A FUNCTION
paragraphs: A function is executed when it is called.
Example: void greet() { cout << "Hello!"; } int main() { greet(); return 0; }

sections.heading: FUNCTION CALL FLOW
paragraphs: Think of a function call as asking a program component to perform a specific task.
list: Program reaches the function call.
Control moves to the function.
Function statements execute.
Function returns control to the calling code.

sections.heading: VOID FUNCTIONS
paragraphs: A void function performs an action but does not return a value.

sections.heading: VALUE-RETURNING FUNCTIONS
paragraphs: A value-returning function sends a result back to the caller.
Example: int square(int number) { return number * number; }

sections.heading: RETURN TYPE
paragraphs: The return type tells C++ what kind of value a function returns.
A return statement should provide a value compatible with the function's return type.
list: int calculate()
double average()
string getName()
bool isValid()
void display()

sections.heading: RETURN STATEMENT
paragraphs: The return statement ends a function and may send a value back.
Example: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
The caller can store the returned value: int sum = add(10, 5);

sections.heading: PARAMETERS
paragraphs: Parameters are variables listed in a function definition.
Example: void greet(string name) { cout << "Hello " << name; }
name is the parameter that receives a value when the function is called.

sections.heading: ARGUMENTS
paragraphs: An argument is the actual value supplied when a function is called.
list: Parameter – definition
Argument – value supplied during the call

sections.heading: MULTIPLE PARAMETERS
paragraphs: A function can have more than one parameter.
Example: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
Call: int result = add(10, 20); cout << result;

sections.heading: ACTIVITY: FUNCTION PARAMETERS
list: It should receive: student name
It should receive: student age
It should receive: student section

sections.heading: PASSING ARGUMENTS BY VALUE
paragraphs: In a simple pass-by-value function call, the function receives a copy of the argument.
Changing x inside the function does not change the original variable passed to it.

sections.heading: PASS-BY-VALUE EXAMPLE
paragraphs: Output remains 10 because x is a copy.

sections.heading: ACTIVITY: TRACE PASS-BY-VALUE
paragraphs: int x = 5; void change(int n) { n = 20; } change(x); cout << x;
Question: What is the output and why?

sections.heading: FUNCTION PROTOTYPES
paragraphs: A function prototype tells the compiler about a function before its definition appears.
Example: int add(int a, int b);
The definition can appear later: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

sections.heading: WHY USE FUNCTION PROTOTYPES?
paragraphs: Function prototypes allow functions to be called before their full definitions appear in the source code.
They improve program organization when functions are placed below main().
Typical structure: Include headers, Function prototypes, main(), Function definitions

sections.heading: PROTOTYPE EXAMPLE
paragraphs: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

sections.heading: FUNCTION OVERVIEW
paragraphs: Functions can be classified by whether they receive parameters and/or return values.
Understanding these combinations helps select the appropriate function design.
list: No parameters, no return value
Parameters, no return value
No parameters, return value
Parameters, return value

sections.heading: TYPE 1: NO PARAMETERS, NO RETURN
paragraphs: The function performs an action without receiving data or returning a result.

sections.heading: TYPE 2: PARAMETERS, NO RETURN
paragraphs: Example: void greet(string name) { cout << "Hello " << name; }
The function receives data but only performs an action.

sections.heading: TYPE 3: NO PARAMETERS, RETURN VALUE
paragraphs: The function does not receive an argument but returns a value.

sections.heading: TYPE 4: PARAMETERS AND RETURN VALUE
paragraphs: Example: int multiply(int a, int b) { return a * b; }

sections.heading: NESTED FUNCTION CALLS
paragraphs: A function can call another function.
Example: int square(int x) { return x * x; } int calculate(int x) { return square(x) + 10; }
Functions can be combined to build larger solutions.

sections.heading: FUNCTIONS AND MODULAR PROGRAMMING
paragraphs: Modular programming divides a program into smaller components.
Each function should ideally perform one clear task.
Example program modules: getInput(), calculateAverage(), displayResult()
Breaking a program into functions makes the solution easier to understand and maintain.

sections.heading: FUNCTIONS: BEST PRACTICES
list: Give functions meaningful names.
Keep each function focused on one task.
Use parameters instead of unnecessary global variables.
Choose an appropriate return type.
Avoid repeating the same code.
Use prototypes when needed.
Keep functions short and readable.

sections.heading: KEY TAKEAWAYS
list: Functions are reusable blocks of code.
A function may receive parameters.
Arguments are values passed to parameters.
A function may return a value or use void.
return sends a result back to the caller.
Function prototypes declare functions before their definitions.
Functions support modular and reusable C++ programs.
Well-designed functions make programs easier to read, test, and maintain.
